pages.description: Three approaches to getting your business found by AI answer engines: passive ranking, reactive scanning, and active page publishing. Understand what each costs, how long it takes, and which suits your market position.
pages.markdown:
# Why AI visibility matters for your business

You have three ways to move your business into AI answers: passive ranking, reactive scanning, or active page publishing. Which suits your market depends on time, budget, and competition.

# Three approaches to getting found by AI

You have three ways to move your business into AI answers:

**Passive ranking.** You publish content on your site and hope Google and AI engines eventually discover and cite it. This costs little upfront but takes months or years, and there's no guarantee your rivals won't occupy that space first.

**Reactive scanning.** You run a free scan to see where AI answers and Google search send buyers to your rivals instead of you. A scan shows the gap between where you rank and where you need to be. It's a one-time measurement—useful for understanding the problem, but it doesn't close the gap.

**Active page publishing.** You write and publish pages built to answer the questions buyers ask AI and Google. [See what AI tells buyers about your market — and write your way in.](https://reachkit.app/) Weekly market re-measurement shows whether your new pages move the needle. [A page written and published for your site every day, your market re-measured every week.](https://reachkit.app/pricing)

Passive ranking suits businesses with time to wait. Reactive scanning suits businesses that need to know where they stand before deciding what to do. Active publishing suits businesses in competitive markets that need visibility now and want to measure whether their work is moving the needle.

# How to choose the right approach for your market

[A free scan shows where AI answers and Google search send buyers to your rivals instead of you.](https://reachkit.app/) Start there if you're unsure of the gap.

If you're in a market where buyers consult AI before searching Google, passive ranking alone won't close the gap fast enough. Rivals are already moving into those answers.

If you want ongoing visibility—not a one-time snapshot—you need weekly re-measurement to know whether your effort is working. The subscription is €49 per month, VAT included, billed in advance through Stripe.

Choose passive ranking if you have months to spare and few competitors publishing to AI engines. Choose reactive scanning if you need to see the problem before you commit to solving it. Choose active publishing if you're in a competitive market and need to know every week whether you're moving closer to where buyers look.

pages.description: Ranking on ChatGPT means getting named when it answers buyer questions. Here's how to check where you stand and start fixing it, step by step.
pages.markdown:
:::answer
Ranking on ChatGPT means being one of the handful of companies it names when someone asks what to use. You get there by finding the questions your buyers ask, checking whether AI answers name you or a rival, then publishing pages on your own site that answer those questions with facts, so there's something for AI to point to.
:::

:::takeaways
- ChatGPT names a small handful of companies per answer, so you need to know which buyer questions it's answering and whether you're in the list.
- A free scan can show how often AI names you versus rivals, and which buyer searches your rivals rank for and you don't.
- Pages written from facts on your own site give ChatGPT something concrete to cite — vague marketing copy doesn't.
- Technical blockers like a blocked AI reader or missing sitemap can keep you out of answers even if your content is good.
- Checking this weekly matters more than checking it once, because the answers change as pages get published and re-crawled.
:::

## What do you need before you start?

You need your own website, access to publish pages on it, and a list of the real questions your buyers type into ChatGPT and Google before they pick a company like yours — not guesses, actual phrasing. You also need a way to see what AI currently says in response to those questions, because you can't fix what you haven't measured.

A [free scan](https://reachkit.app/) shows where AI answers and Google search send buyers to your rivals instead of you. That one check gives you the starting point: which questions get asked, who gets named, and where your own site falls short technically. Without it you're writing pages against guesses about what buyers ask, which wastes the time you're trying to save.

You'll also want patience for a slower kind of progress. This isn't a setting you flip — it's pages published and re-crawled over weeks, so plan to check progress on a schedule rather than expecting a single fix to move the needle overnight.

## What are the steps to rank on ChatGPT?

Ranking on ChatGPT comes down to finding out what it currently says, then giving it better material to say instead. Here's the order that works.

1. **Run a scan of your site and market.** This shows how often AI currently names you and which rivals it names instead. One such measurement found that on 5 October 2026, AI answers named reachkit.app for 0 of the 11 buyer questions they answered — a result that only becomes visible once you measure it.
2. **List the buyer questions AI is answering.** These are phrased the way a buyer thinks, not the way your homepage is written — "best X for Y" or "how does X work," not your tagline.
3. **Check which rivals get named for each question.** A scan logs this per question. In the same measurement, AI answers cited otterly.ai for [1](https://reachkit.app/) of the 11 buyer questions and rankscale.ai for 1 of the 11 — showing that even narrow, specific citations are how these answers work, not broad brand mentions.
4. **Fix technical blockers first.** A blocked AI reader, a missing title tag, no sitemap, or a slow page can keep a page out of consideration before content quality even matters.
5. **Write one page per question, from facts on your own site.** Each page should answer a single buyer question plainly, using real details — prices, features, specifics — rather than general claims, since AI answers need something concrete to point to.
6. **Publish on your own domain, in your own voice.** The page has to live where the facts live, so it can be checked and cited.
7. **Review before it goes live.** Every page should wait a day for you to read it — or stop it — before it goes live, so nothing goes out that doesn't represent your business accurately.
8. **Re-measure weekly.** A single scan tells you where you stand today; a weekly re-measure of your whole market tells you whether the pages you published are changing what AI says.

## How do you check whether it worked?

You check by re-running the same measurement and comparing the count of questions where you're named now against where you started. A single improvement — say, moving from 0 named questions to even 1 or 2 — is a real, countable signal, not a vague sense that things feel better.

Look specifically at the questions you targeted with new pages, not just an overall score. If you wrote a page answering a specific buyer question and AI still doesn't cite it a week or two later, that page likely needs stronger facts, clearer structure, or the underlying technical issue hasn't been fixed yet.

Also check which rivals still get named instead of you on those same questions. If a competitor keeps showing up for a question your new page targets, that tells you the gap between their page and yours — often it's specificity: a rival's page states a number or a feature plainly where yours still speaks in generalities.

## What mistakes should you avoid?

The most common mistake is writing content aimed at how your business wants to describe itself rather than the exact question a buyer typed. AI answers respond to the question asked, not to a slogan near it, so content needs to open with a direct answer to a stated question, not a brand pitch.

Another mistake is skipping the technical check. A page full of good facts still won't get read if AI readers are blocked, there's no sitemap, or the page loads too slowly — these are often invisible to a site owner but visible in a scan, so check this before you spend time writing.

A third mistake is publishing once and expecting a lasting result. AI answers shift as new pages get crawled across the whole market, including your rivals' pages, so a one-time push fades without a weekly re-measure to confirm the gain held and to catch new gaps opening up.

Last, don't skip reading what you publish. Rushing pages live without a review step risks a page that states something inaccurate about your own business — far worse for trust than being unranked.

## What should you do next?

Start with the scan, since it's free and it tells you exactly where you stand before you write anything: how often AI names you, which rivals it names instead, and what's blocking you technically. From there, you know which buyer questions to prioritize first.

If you'd rather not write and publish each page yourself, [one plan — one page a day](https://reachkit.app/pricing) covers a page written and published for your site every day, plus a weekly re-measure of your whole market, for €49 a month, VAT included. Each page waits a day for you to approve or stop before it goes live, so you keep control over what represents your business.

If you want to see what this looks like before committing to anything, [every free scan is published in the open](https://reachkit.app/scans) — worth a look to see the kind of gaps a scan surfaces for other sites in this position.

- [Terms](https://reachkit.app/terms)

Run the [free scan](https://reachkit.app/) first — it shows exactly which buyer questions you're missing from before you write a single page.

- Pages written from facts on your own site, published on your own schedule, are what close the gap over time.
- A weekly re-measure tells you whether the pages you publish are changing who gets named.
:::

## What do you need before you start?

You need your own site, a way to see what AI answers currently say about your market, and a willingness to publish pages regularly rather than once. Ranking in AI Overview is not a one-time fix — it depends on having facts on your own site that an AI engine can read and cite, and on knowing which questions your buyers ask.

That scan also shows how often AI names you and which rivals it names instead, so you're not guessing at the gap — you're looking at it.

You also need patience with the mechanics: AI engines answer from pages that already exist and already say something specific. If your site has no page answering a given buyer question, there is nothing for the engine to cite. That's the gap the rest of this page walks you through closing.

## What are the steps to rank in AI Overview?

The path runs from measuring where you stand today to publishing pages that close the gaps, then checking weekly whether the gap is closing. Each step below is drawn from how ReachKit's own process works, and what the facts show it does.

1. **Run a free scan of your site.** A free scan shows where AI answers and Google search send buyers to your rivals instead of you — result: you get a concrete list of the questions where a rival is named and you are not.
2. **Read your Discoverability Score.** [ReachKit measured reachkit.app on 5 October 2026 and gave it a Discoverability Score of 18 out of 100](https://reachkit.app/scan/reachkit.app) — result: one number tells you how findable you are right now, so you have a baseline to improve against.
3. **Check which engines were asked and which weren't.** ReachKit's measurement of reachkit.app on 5 October 2026 read Google's top ten results and the answers of Google AI Overview, Google AI Mode and ChatGPT; it does not measure Perplexity — result: you know exactly which engines your score covers, and that Perplexity sits outside it.
4. **See how often you're named versus a rival.** On 5 October 2026, AI answers named reachkit.app for 0 of the 10 buyer questions they answered in ReachKit's measurement, while on the same date AI answers cited zapier.com for 3 of the 10 buyer questions — result: you see the exact scoreboard, not a vague sense of falling behind.

6. **Get your first page proposed.** Every scan comes with your first page, proposed and free — result: you don't start from a blank page; you start from a specific answer to a specific gap.
7. **Publish one page a day against the gaps found.** A page written and published for your site every day, your market re-measured — result: each day closes one more question where a rival was named and you weren't.
8. **Review before it goes live.** Every page waits a day for you to read it — or stop it — before it goes live — result: you keep control over what's published under your name, with 24 hours to stop any page.
9. **Let the weekly re-measure run.** Your market is re-measured every week — result: you get a repeated, comparable check on whether the gap between you and rivals like zapier.com and position.digital is narrowing.
10. **Read the weekly movement email.** A weekly movement email tells you what changed — result: you see week over week whether new pages are moving the needle, without having to run your own checks.

## How do you check it worked?

You check by re-reading your Discoverability Score and by watching whether AI answers start naming you for the questions they previously gave to rivals. The score and the named-versus-not count are the two numbers that tell you anything changed.

On 5 October 2026, AI answers named reachkit.app for 0 of the 10 buyer questions measured, while citing zapier.com for 3 and position.digital for 2 of those same questions. That's the kind of gap you're watching close: not a general sense of "more visibility," but a specific count of named-or-not against specific rivals, repeated weekly. Each filled row in that comparison is a rival being recommended — your goal is to turn filled rows into your own name.

The weekly re-measure is what makes this checkable at all. Without a repeated, dated measurement, you're left guessing whether a new page helped. With it, you get a weekly movement email that shows what moved, so the check is built into the process rather than something you have to do by hand.

## What mistakes should you avoid?

The most common mistake is writing generic pages instead of pages that answer the specific questions your buyers ask and that rivals currently own. A page that doesn't match a real buyer question gives an AI engine nothing to cite it for.

- **Guessing at keywords instead of measuring questions.** Without a scan, you're optimizing for what you assume buyers ask, not what they type into ChatGPT or Google AI Mode.

- **Publishing once and stopping.** Ranking is tracked by weekly re-measure, not a single snapshot; a single page rarely closes a gap that a rival has owned for months.
- **Writing from nothing.** Content that isn't written from facts on your own site, in your own voice, has nothing specific for an AI engine to quote back to a buyer.
- **Skipping the review step.** Every page waits a day for you to read it or stop it before it goes live — skip that check and you risk publishing something under your name that you didn't verify.
- **Measuring only Google.** Remember the scan reads Google's top ten results alongside Google AI Overview, Google AI Mode and ChatGPT, but not Perplexity — if Perplexity matters to your buyers, you'll need to watch that separately.

## What should you do next?

From there, the next step is steady: one page a day, written from facts on your own site, re-measured every week so you can see the gap with rivals narrow rather than guess at it.

Profound's page mentions [AI Marketer credits for your whole team](https://www.tryprofound.com/pricing), which ties cost to usage rather than a flat seat price.

Profound is an AI visibility tracker aimed at marketing teams who want to see how brands appear across AI answers. Its own pricing page is no longer fully transparent: it emphasizes customized enterprise pricing, while third-party reviewers still surface a roughly [$99 Starter and $399 Growth signal, with Enterprise custom and demo-led](https://deepsmith.ai/blog/profound-alternatives). A separate summary states plainly that [Profound's entry-level package starts at $99/month](https://bbkmarketing.com/2026/06/24/8-top-profound-alternatives-your-marketing-team-can-actually-use/), with [the Growth plan at $399/month](https://bbkmarketing.com/2026/06/24/8-top-profound-alternatives-your-marketing-team-can-actually-use/).

Its pricing page also lists [50 prompts run daily for 7 days](https://www.tryprofound.com/pricing) and tracking across [ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews](https://www.tryprofound.com/pricing), plus [Limited AI Marketer credits](https://www.tryprofound.com/pricing) on lower tiers. Profound suits a marketing team with budget for a demo-led enterprise tool and a need to track a large prompt volume across those three engines specifically. Its limit: pricing above the entry tier is not published, so you negotiate rather than read a number and sign up.

## What does Otterly offer?

Otterly is a tracking tool priced in public tiers, which makes it easier to compare than Profound's demo-led upper tiers. Its Standard plan is listed at [$ 189 /month](https://otterly.ai/pricing), and its Premium tier at [$ 489 /month](https://otterly.ai/pricing), with an Enterprise tier described as [Enterprise Custom Starting from 1,000 search prompts](https://otterly.ai/pricing).

Otterly's features page states it [Tracks all 7 major AI search engines](https://otterly.ai/features) and [Monitors 65+ countries and languages](https://otterly.ai/features), and its pricing page notes [Unlimited team members](https://otterly.ai/pricing) on its plans. A third-party summary adds that its Lite plan is [$29 per month (or $25 annual) for 15 tracked prompts across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and Microsoft Copilot](https://deepsmith.ai/blog/profound-alternatives). Otterly suits a team that wants broad engine and language coverage and is willing to add paid extras for full engine access at the entry tier. Its limit: the full seven-engine claim on its features page does not match its own pricing page, where Claude, Google AI Mode and Gemini are paid extras on the Standard plan.

## What does ReachKit offer?

ReachKit is built for a founder or business owner who wants to know where AI answers and Google send buyers instead of to them, and then do something about it. The subscription is [€49 per month, VAT included, billed in advance through Stripe](https://content.reachkit.app/best-answer-engine-optimization-services-for-ai-visibility), covering one page published for your site every day, new or updated, and your market re-measured every week.

We run 12 searches in Google that buyers in your market make, and record who is on the first page of each. Every Monday we ask Google AI Mode and ChatGPT the 25 questions a buyer in your market would ask, each one twice, because AI answers change from one run to the next. ReachKit suits a small business or service business that wants a flat price and pages published, not just a report. Its limit: it does not track Perplexity, so a business whose buyers rely heavily on that engine sees a gap in coverage.

## Which one should you choose?

Choose Otterly if your buyers are spread across Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot and you want one dashboard covering both, and you have budget past the [$189](https://deepsmith.ai/blog/profound-alternatives) a month Standard tier once you add the engines you need. Otterly's own [features page](https://otterly.ai/features) names Perplexity and Copilot explicitly, which neither Profound's pricing page nor ReachKit's tracking list does.

Choose Profound if you run a marketing team that wants a high daily prompt volume, specifically [50 prompts run daily for 7 days](https://www.tryprofound.com/pricing), and you're comfortable with enterprise pricing settled by demo rather than published upfront.

Choose ReachKit if you want one flat price, a weekly re-measure of your whole market, and a page written and published for your site every day rather than a dashboard alone. That suits a small business, local business or e-commerce site that doesn't have a marketing team to act on what a tracker reports.
